questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of universal instantiation?
questions.explanation: Universal instantiation allows us to take a universally quantified statement and apply it to a specific instance. Option (a) correctly demonstrates this by inferring \( P(a) \) from \( \forall x \, P(x) \).

distractorRationale.b: This is an example of existential generalisation.
distractorRationale.c: This is incorrect because it assumes a specific instance from an existential statement.
distractorRationale.d: This is an application of modus ponens, not universal instantiation.

questions.stem: Given the premises \( \forall x \, (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)) \) and \( P(c) \), what can be concluded?
questions.explanation: By applying universal instantiation to \( \forall x \, (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)) \), we get \( P(c) \rightarrow Q(c) \). Given \( P(c) \), we can use modus ponens to conclude \( Q(c) \).

distractorRationale.b: This conclusion is not directly supported by the premises.
distractorRationale.c: This is an overgeneralization; the premises do not support a universal conclusion.
distractorRationale.d: The premises do not provide enough information to conclude both \( P(c) \) and \( Q(c) \).

questions.stem: If \( \forall x \, (P(x) \rightarrow R(x)) \) and \( \exists x \, (P(x) \land \neg R(x)) \), how many individuals can satisfy both premises simultaneously? Provide your answer as an integer.
questions.explanation: The first premise states that for all individuals, if \( P(x) \) is true, then \( R(x) \) must also be true. The second premise claims there exists an individual for which \( P(x) \) is true and \( R(x) \) is false. These premises are contradictory, so no individual can satisfy both simultaneously.

questions.stem: Which rule allows you to conclude \( \exists x \, P(x) \) from \( P(a) \)?
questions.explanation: Existential generalisation allows us to infer the existence of an individual with a property if we know a specific individual has that property. Thus, from \( P(a) \), we can conclude \( \exists x \, P(x) \).

distractorRationale.a: Universal instantiation is used to derive specific instances from universal statements.
distractorRationale.c: Modus ponens is a rule of inference for implications, not quantifiers.
distractorRationale.d: Universal generalisation is used to infer a universal statement from specific instances, not existential.

questions.explanation: If \( \forall x \, P(x) \) is true, then \( P(x) \) holds for every individual \( x \). Therefore, \( P(a) \) must be true for any specific \( a \).

questions.stem: Given \( \forall x \, (P(x) \lor Q(x)) \) and \( \neg P(a) \), how many individuals can be concluded to satisfy \( Q(x) \)? Provide your answer as an integer.
questions.explanation: From \( \forall x \, (P(x) \lor Q(x)) \), we know that for every individual \( x \), either \( P(x) \) or \( Q(x) \) must be true. Given \( \neg P(a) \), it follows that \( Q(a) \) must be true. Therefore, at least one individual, \( a \), satisfies \( Q(x) \).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is equivalent to \( \neg \forall x \, P(x) \)?
questions.explanation: The negation of a universal quantifier \( \forall x \, P(x) \) is equivalent to the existence of an \( x \) for which \( P(x) \) is false, i.e., \( \exists x \, \neg P(x) \).

questions.stem: Construct a formal proof to show that from \( \forall x \, (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)) \) and \( \exists x \, P(x) \), it follows that \( \exists x \, Q(x) \).
markingGuide: Apply universal instantiation to \( \forall x \, (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)) \) to obtain \( P(a) \rightarrow Q(a) \) for some \( a \).
Use the existential premise \( \exists x \, P(x) \) to assert \( P(a) \) for some \( a \).
Apply modus ponens to conclude \( Q(a) \).
Use existential generalisation to conclude \( \exists x \, Q(x) \).
questions.explanation: To prove \( \exists x \, Q(x) \), we start by applying universal instantiation to \( \forall x \, (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)) \), giving us \( P(a) \rightarrow Q(a) \) for some \( a \). From \( \exists x \, P(x) \), we know \( P(a) \) is true for some \( a \). Using modus ponens, we conclude \( Q(a) \). Finally, by existential generalisation, we conclude \( \exists x \, Q(x) \).
